61: Reading the Law
62: Text in small capitals defines key terms.
63: Text in italics gives reminders and clarifi­
64: cations. Faction icons mark rules modified

66: Root contains two rulebooks: the Learning to Play guide
67: and this book, the Law. If you like a conversational
68: teaching style and many graphical examples, read the
69: Learning to Play guide. If you like a strictly defined,
70: formal rules in a concise reference style, read the Law.
71: These rules of thumb will help you interpret the Law.
72: Q1. I’d like to do something, and the rules don’t say
73: that I can’t do it. Can I do it?
74: A1. Within the confines of the action, yes! The game will often
75: surprise you with outlandish, unexpected situations, and that’s
76: part of the fun, but this doesn’t mean you can flip the table.
77: Q2. It seems like something should happen, but the
78: rule doesn’t tell me to do that thing. What do I do?
79: A2. Follow the literal word of the Law, not your instinct, even
80: if a similar rule exists.
81: Q3. A rule uses a specific term or action. Does it also
82: include another, closely related term or action?
83: A3. Nope! Assume we mean only the original term and not
84: any related terms. For example, the terms move and place
85: are different. For specific term definitions, see the Glossary
86: (Appendix G).
87: If you have any other questions, check our website for
88: more answers: ledergames.com/root
89: If you have any missing or damaged components, you
90: can go here for support: ledergames.com/replacements
91: If you have questions about specific cards, go to the

93: 1. Golden Rules
94: This chapter gives answers to technical, detailed ques­
95: tions. You do not need to read it when first learning.
96: 1.1 Rules Conflicts
97: 1.1.1     Precedence. If a card conflicts with the Law, fol­
98: low the card. If the Learning to Play guide con­
99: flicts with the Law, follow the Law. If you can fol­
100: low both a general rule and a faction or hireling
101: rule, follow both; if you cannot, follow the faction
102: or hireling rule.
103: 1.1.2     Use of Cannot. The term cannot is absolute. It
104: cannot be overridden unless explicitly instructed.
105: 1.1.3     Unclear Resolutions and Choices. Whenever it
106: is unclear what order simultaneous effects should
107: resolve in, or which player should make a deci­
108: sion, the player taking their turn chooses.
109: 1.2 Public and Private Information
110: 1.2.1     Hands. Players may only show or reveal cards in
111: their hand if explicitly instructed, but the number
112: of cards in their hand is public information. O
113: 1.2.2     Piles and the Shared Deck. Face-up piles such
114: as the discard pile can be searched and inspected.
115: The shared deck cannot.
116: 1.3 Negotiation, Deals, and Consent
117: 1.3.1     Agreements. Players may discuss the game and
118: make agreements, but they are non-binding.
119: 1.3.2     Cards. Players may only give cards to each other
120: if explicitly instructed.
121: 1.3.3     Consent. Actions never require consent.
122: 1.4 Game Structure
123: 1.4.1     Turn Structure. Each player’s turn has three
124: phases: Birdsong, Daylight, and Evening. Any­
125: thing that says “at start of” a phase happens be­
126: fore everything else in the phase, and anything
127: that says “at end of” happens after everything else
128: in the phase but before the start of the next phase,
129: if any. After a player ends Evening, the next clock­
130: wise player begins their turn. Play continues until
131: one player has won the game (3.1).
132: 1.4.2     Interrupts. You cannot interrupt an action (in­
133: cluding a compound action such as the Marquise’s
134: March), ability (such as the Corvids’ Exposure), or
135: persistent effect (such as the Eyrie Emigre card) with
136: another effect unless it explicitly allows it. (For ex­
137: ample, the Armorers card says it is used “In battle...”).
138: 1.4.3     End of Turn. Once a player begins the last step of
139: their turn, they cannot take actions except those
140: that specify “end of Evening” or “end of turn,”
141: such as hirelings (Appendix H).
142: 1.5 Pieces
143: 1.5.1     Limits. Pieces are limited by the contents of the
144: game. Do not use proxy pieces if you run out.
145: 1.5.2     Starting Faction. Each player owns the faction
146: they choose in setup (5) and the pieces listed on
147: the back of its faction board except for items. Ge­
148: nerically, these are called faction pieces or sim­
149: ilar. Specifically, these are called [faction name]
150: pieces. (For example, “your faction warriors” and
151: “warriors of your faction” and “Marquise warriors” all
152: refer to the orange wooden cat-shaped warriors.)
153: 1.5.3     Piece Ownership. The ownership of faction piec­
154: es cannot change. (For example, the Marquise can­
155: not use Field Hospitals on Riverfolk mercenaries or
156: hirelings, since these are not Marquise warriors.)
157: 1.5.4     Piece Manipulation. Pieces are placed and re­
158: moved as defined in the Glossary (G.20, G.24). If
159: you are prompted to place, take, or remove pieces
160: but you cannot do so fully, you must place, take, or
161: remove the maximum number possible. (This does
162: not let you avoid costs or prerequisites. You just cannot
163: do less than the most you can.) If multiple pieces  are

185: 3. Victory
186: 3.1 How to Win
187: The first player to reach 30 victory points immediately
188: wins the game.
189: 3.1.1     Ties. If multiple players reach 30 victory points si­
190: multaneously, the tied player closest in clockwise
191: order to the current player wins. (This includes the
192: current player.)
193: 3.2 Scoring Victory Points
194: Each faction has a unique way to score victory points,
195: but any faction can score victory points as follows.
196: 3.2.1     Removing Buildings and Tokens. Whenever you
197: remove an enemy’s building or token, you score
198: one victory point.
199: 3.2.2     Crafting Items. Whenever you craft an item (4.1),
200: score the victory points listed on the card. EHS

212: nance card at the start of your Birdsong.

215: ners at the start of your Birdsong.
